passages.title: A School Without Walls
passages.text:
In 2013, an Indian scientist named Sugata Mitra won a large prize for an unusual idea. Years earlier, he had made a hole in the wall between his office and a poor neighbourhood in New Delhi and placed a computer with an internet connection inside it. He did not explain anything; he simply left it there and watched what happened.

Within hours, curious children had gathered around the screen. None of them had used a computer before, and many spoke very little English. Yet within a few days they had learned to open programs, browse the internet and teach each other what they had discovered. Mitra repeated the experiment in other villages and cities and found similar results. He called this way of learning 'minimally invasive education', which means that adults step back and let children explore.

Mitra later created what he called 'Schools in the Cloud'. These are rooms with computers where groups of children work on big questions, such as 'Why do we dream?' or 'Can trees think?'. Instead of giving answers, an adult volunteer, often a retired teacher connected by video, encourages **them** and asks further questions. Mitra believes that children working in groups can find out far more than adults expect.

Not everyone agrees. Some teachers argue that children still need a structured lesson plan and that information found online is not always accurate. Others worry that without guidance, shy children may be left out. Even so, Mitra's experiments have made many educators think again about how much children can learn on their own.
